newsitem.title: SPAIN: Bank of Spain seen cutting rates after 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Spain seen cutting rates after 1997 budget.

text.p: The Bank of Spain will keep its key money market interest rate unchanged on Friday, withholding its sixth reduction of the year until the government unveils its 1997 budget draft at month's end, economists said.

The administration has pledged to present a stringent plan that will slash the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product from an estimated 4.4 percent this year, enabling Spain to join in the launch of Europe's common currency.
Economists believe that on Friday the central bank will keep its rate at 7.25 percent at the regular repurchase tender, waiting for proof the government is adhering to its vow.

"The Bank of Spain wants to see confirmation in the budget of a restrictive fiscal policy. Any possible (rate) cut is linked to the budget," said Marisol de Francisco, economist at Analistas Financieros Internacionales (AFI).
A reduction in the deficit and in public expenditure helps curb inflation, the central task of monetary authorities.
Given a dearth of information on the outlines of the budget, analysts said there would be little logic to an interest rate cut on Friday.
Indeed, conditions may have worsened since the last regular money market intervention or repo 10 days ago, which might have been an opportune date if the central bank harboured no budget worries.
But economists said that now the central bank may face deterioration in two of its main indicators, making a reduction difficult to justify .
Inflation is expected to have risen to 3.9 percent in August after 3.7 percent in July, bloated by emergency government taxes on cigarettes and tobacco.

"There are two indicators which are expected to be bad: August inflation and July public deficit data. With these figures and the budget pending, it's not the ideal time to cut interest rates", said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.

Nonetheless, Spanish economists expect the Bank of Spain to be satisfied with the government's proposal and to cut the rate in the next three to four weeks. One-month forward rate agreements are discounting a rate cut in just over one month.
In a Reuters poll, nine of 10 financial experts surveyed expected the central bank to keep rates unchanged on Friday.

In all, market thinking has it that the central bank is eyeing a relaxation of monetary policy as a way of boosting economic activity, but without dropping its guard against inflation and the state deficit.
Most think the central bank may cut at the start of October, but opinions differ on the possible size.
"There's room for two 25 basis point cuts," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

AFI's De Francisco thinks there could be one 50 basis points move immediately after the budget, while Societe Generale's Urrutia gives a margin of 50-75 basis points, with a first cut of 25 basis points.
The Bank of Spain last lowered its rate in June, bringing it down to the current 7.25 percent from nine percent at the beginning of January.
